newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan pins tourism hopes on peace and advertising.
newsitem.headline: Jordan pins tourism hopes on peace and advertising.

text.p: Jordan's tourism industry is pinning hopes for a 1997 revival on snappier promotion and sustained progress in Middle East peace talks after renewed violence thwarted its ambitions last year.

Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Saleh Irsheidat said on Wednesday the government, aiming to boost tourist numbers by over 15 percent from last year's 1.10 million arrivals, would hand over advertising and marketing to the private sector.
It would also coordinate closely with its former foe Israel in promoting the region as a tourist destination.
"We could have an increase of 15 to 20 percent at least, if things are quiet in the area," Irsheidat told Reuters.

Last year Jordan forecast a boom as figures for the first five months showed visitors up by 17 percent. But Israeli raids on Lebanon, violence in the West Bank and bread riots in southern Jordan scared people away and the final 1996 numbers were only 2.8 percent higher than 1995.
Irsheidat said 1996 revenues of 770 million dinars ($1.09 billion) were up around 10 percent.

He said Jordan had seen $500 million invested in tourism since its 1994 peace treaty with Israel, including 4,500 new hotel rooms completed or under construction. Most was spent in southern Jordan around the Nabatean rock city of Petra and the Red Sea port of Aqaba. Longer-term plans include joint projects with Israel at the Dead Sea, the lowest point on Earth.

Despite a cooling of political relations with Israel since the election last May of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Irsheidat said the two countries needed to cooperate if Jordan was to get a good return on its investment.
"We agreed to work together in a promotion programme around the world," he said. "The Israelis are so strong in America... and they could benefit from our market in southeast Asia."
He said the two countries had launched a joint promotion in Thailand. Tourists from Asia would fly on Royal Jordanian flights to Jordan before moving on to Israel.

Earlier this month Jordan, Israel and the Palestinian Authority launched a joint 'Holy Land' advertising campaign in the United States to capitalise on the rare glow of Middle East rapprochement after Palestinians and Israelis agreed on limited Palestinian self-rule in the volatile town of Hebron.
Irsheidat said the Hebron agreement might draw some tourists who cancelled last year. But further violence or tension could threaten the peak spring and autumn seasons.
"Still we've got a chance. We got a lot of cancellations last year...It depends on the aftermath of the peace between the Israelis and the Palestinians," he said.
Jordan's parliament is due to discuss an amendment to the tourism law next week that would transfer responsibility for promotion to the private sector.
"We have already established the Jordanian Tourism Board...comprising private sector companies which would lead the campaign," he said.
He said the companies, including hotels and tourist firms as well as state-owned Royal Jordanian airlines, would get state funds but would have to come up with extra cash themselves.
"The private sector are quicker than government and they might have more specific ideas," Irsheidat said.
Jordan, banking on continued rises in tourism numbers, plans to almost double the number of hotel beds to 18,000 by the year 2000 from 9,400 last year.
